questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a single-gene disorder with autosomal dominant inheritance?

options.explanation: Huntington disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene and follows autosomal dominant inheritance.
Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene.
Sickle cell anemia is autosomal recessive, due to a point mutation in the HBB gene.
Tay-Sachs is autosomal recessive, caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency.
Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, due to factor VIII deficiency.

explanation.overview: Autosomal dominant disorders require only one mutant allele to cause disease. Huntington disease is a classic example.
explanation.highYield: Remember: Huntington is autosomal dominant; CF and sickle cell are recessive; hemophilia is X-linked.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic counseling and presymptomatic testing are available for Huntington disease.

questions.question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in which gene?

options.explanation: CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene on chromosome 7 is mutated in cystic fibrosis.
Dystrophin mutations cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
FMR1 mutations cause Fragile X syndrome.
BRCA1 mutations are associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

explanation.overview: CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene on chromosome 7 is mutated in cystic fibrosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Newborn screening and genetic testing are used for diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an autosomal recessive disorder?

options.explanation: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, caused by FBN1 mutations.
Phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive due to PAH gene mutations.
Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant, caused by FGFR3 mutations.
Myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant, caused by CTG repeat expansion.

explanation.overview: Phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive. Marfan, NF1, achondroplasia, and myotonic dystrophy are autosomal dominant.
explanation.highYield: PKU is autosomal recessive; most inborn errors of metabolism are recessive.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Newborn screening for PKU allows early dietary intervention.

questions.question: X-linked recessive disorders are more common in:

options.explanation: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive mutation on the X chromosome causes disease. Females require two copies.
Females need two mutant alleles to be affected, making it less common.
Females can be carriers or affected if homozygous.
While males are more common, affected females can occur (homozygous).

explanation.overview: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive mutation on the X chromosome causes disease. Females require two copies.
explanation.highYield: X-linked recessive disorders affect males more often.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis are offered in at-risk families.

questions.question: Which of the following is an X-linked recessive disorder?

options.explanation: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Duchenne MD is X-linked recessive, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Fragile X is X-linked (usually dominant with anticipation), but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Hemophilia A (factor VIII), Duchenne MD (dystrophin), and Fragile X (FMR1) are all X-linked.
There are multiple X-linked disorders listed.

explanation.overview: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency), Duchenne MD (dystrophin), and Fragile X (FMR1) are all X-linked.
explanation.highYield: Classic X-linked recessive: hemophilia A, Duchenne MD, G6PD deficiency.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Family history is key for diagnosis and genetic counseling.

questions.question: The concept of 'anticipation' refers to:

options.text: Increasing severity of disease in successive generations
options.explanation: This is part of anticipation, but the full definition includes earlier onset and repeat expansion.
Also part of anticipation, but the comprehensive answer is 'All of the above'.

options.text: Due to expansion of trinucleotide repeats
options.explanation: Molecular mechanism, but anticipation encompasses the clinical phenomenon.
Anticipation is seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy, where repeats expand and disease worsens.

explanation.overview: Anticipation is seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy, where repeats expand and disease worsens.
explanation.highYield: Anticipation = earlier onset + increased severity in subsequent generations.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing can predict repeat size and risk of anticipation.

questions.question: Which of the following disorders exhibits anticipation?

options.explanation: Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
All are trinucleotide repeat disorders with anticipation.
There are multiple disorders with anticipation.

explanation.overview: All are trinucleotide repeat disorders with anticipation.
explanation.highYield: Trinucleotide repeat disorders: Huntington (CAG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), fragile X (CGG).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Anticipation explains why age at onset decreases in successive generations.

questions.question: The mutation in Huntington disease is:

options.text: CAG repeat expansion in HTT gene
options.explanation: Huntington disease is caused by CAG (polyglutamine) repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene.

options.text: CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene
options.explanation: CTG repeat in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy.

options.text: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 gene
options.explanation: CGG repeat in FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome.
Deletion in dystrophin causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
CFTR point mutations cause cystic fibrosis.

explanation.overview: Huntington disease is caused by CAG (polyglutamine) repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing for CAG repeat length is available for at-risk individuals.

questions.question: Myotonic dystrophy is associated with which repeat?

options.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 involves CTG expansion in the DMPK gene.
CAG in HTT causes Huntington disease.
CGG in FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome.
GAA in frataxin causes Friedreich ataxia.
CCG in FMR2 is associated with FRAXE, not myotonic dystrophy.

explanation.overview: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 involves CTG expansion in the DMPK gene.
explanation.highYield: Myotonic dystrophy = CTG repeat in DMPK.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Anticipation is prominent; repeat length correlates with severity.

questions.question: Fragile X syndrome is caused by:

options.text: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 gene
options.explanation: Fragile X results from CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, leading to silencing.
CAG repeats are seen in Huntington and other polyglutamine disorders.
Deletion of 15q11 is associated with Prader-Willi/Angelman syndromes.
UPD is involved in imprinting disorders, not fragile X.

explanation.overview: Fragile X results from CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, leading to silencing.
explanation.highYield: Fragile X = CGG repeat in FMR1.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Males are more severely affected; females can have variable expression due to X-inactivation.

questions.question: The most common lethal genetic disorder in Caucasians is:

options.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is the most common fatal autosomal recessive disorder in Caucasians.
Sickle cell is more common in African ancestry.
Tay-Sachs is more common in Ashkenazi Jewish population.
Duchenne is X-linked and less common overall.
Hemophilia A is X-linked and less common.

explanation.overview: Cystic fibrosis is the most common fatal autosomal recessive disorder in Caucasians.
explanation.highYield: CF is the most common lethal genetic disease in Caucasians.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Newborn screening and early intervention improve outcomes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a disorder caused by trinucleotide repeat expansion in a non-coding region?

options.explanation: Fragile X has CGG repeat in the 5' UTR (non-coding).
Myotonic dystrophy has CTG repeat in the 3' UTR (non-coding).
Friedreich ataxia has GAA repeat in an intron (non-coding).
Fragile X (5' UTR), myotonic dystrophy (3' UTR), and Friedreich ataxia (intronic) all have non-coding repeats.

explanation.overview: Fragile X (5' UTR), myotonic dystrophy (3' UTR), and Friedreich ataxia (intronic) all have non-coding repeats.
explanation.highYield: Non-coding repeats: fragile X (CGG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), Friedreich (GAA).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Molecular testing can identify these expansions.

questions.question: Friedreich ataxia is caused by:

options.text: GAA repeat expansion in frataxin gene
options.explanation: Friedreich ataxia involves GAA expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene, impairing mitochondrial function.
CAG repeat expansions are seen in polyglutamine disorders (e.g., Huntington).
Friedreich is due to repeat expansion, not deletion.

explanation.overview: Friedreich ataxia involves GAA expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene, impairing mitochondrial function.
explanation.highYield: Friedreich ataxia = GAA repeat in FXN.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Presents with ataxia, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes.

questions.question: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in which gene?

options.explanation: Marfan syndrome results from fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations, affecting connective tissue.
COL3A1 mutations cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
TGFBR1 mutations are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
FBN2 mutations cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly, not Marfan.

explanation.overview: Marfan syndrome results from fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations, affecting connective tissue.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiovascular complications (aortic root dilation) are the main cause of mortality.

questions.question: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (classic type) is often due to mutations in:

options.explanation: Classic EDS involves type V collagen defects. Vascular EDS involves COL3A1.

explanation.overview: Classic EDS involves type V collagen defects. Vascular EDS involves COL3A1.
explanation.highYield: Classic EDS = COL5A1/COL5A2; vascular EDS = COL3A1.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vascular EDS has high risk of arterial rupture.

questions.question: Osteogenesis imperfecta is most commonly caused by mutations in:

options.explanation: OI is caused by defects in type I collagen, leading to brittle bones.
Type II collagen defects cause chondrodysplasias.
Type III collagen defects cause vascular EDS.
Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome.

explanation.overview: OI is caused by defects in type I collagen, leading to brittle bones.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Clinical severity varies widely; bisphosphonates are used for treatment.

questions.question: Alport syndrome is caused by mutations in:

options.explanation: Alport syndrome (X-linked) is due to COL4A5 mutations affecting basement membrane in kidney, ear, and eye.
Type I collagen defects cause OI.
Type III collagen defects cause vascular EDS.
Laminin defects are seen in some forms of muscular dystrophy.

explanation.overview: Alport syndrome (X-linked) is due to COL4A5 mutations affecting basement membrane in kidney, ear, and eye.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Presents with hematuria, hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities.

questions.question: The most common trisomy in liveborn infants is:

options.explanation: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common viable autosomal aneuploidy.
Trisomy 18 is less common and usually lethal.
Turner syndrome is a monosomy, not a trisomy.
Klinefelter is a sex chromosome aneuploidy, not a trisomy in the usual sense.

explanation.overview: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common viable autosomal aneuploidy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Risk increases with maternal age; prenatal screening is available.

questions.question: The risk of Down syndrome increases with:

options.explanation: Maternal age is the primary risk factor for nondisjunction in meiosis I.
Paternal age is not a significant risk factor for Down syndrome.
Only maternal age is the main risk.
Maternal age is a well-established risk factor.
Paternal age is not a risk factor.

explanation.overview: Maternal age is the primary risk factor for nondisjunction in meiosis I.
explanation.highYield: Down syndrome risk ↑ with maternal age.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prenatal screening and amniocentesis are offered to older mothers.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Down syndrome?

options.text: Flat facial profile, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease
options.explanation: Down syndrome features: brachycephaly, flat facies, epicanthal folds, simian crease, and intellectual disability.
These are features of trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).
These are features of trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).
These are features of Turner syndrome.
These are features of Klinefelter or Marfan syndrome.

explanation.overview: Down syndrome features: brachycephaly, flat facies, epicanthal folds, simian crease, and intellectual disability.
explanation.highYield: Down syndrome = flat facies, epicanthal folds, simian crease.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac defects (AVSD) and GI anomalies are common.

questions.question: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is associated with:

options.text: Rocker-bottom feet, low-set ears, clenched fists
options.explanation: Trisomy 18 features: intrauterine growth retardation, micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and overlapping fingers.

options.text: Webbed neck, short stature, gonadal dysgenesis
options.explanation: These are features of Turner syndrome.

options.text: Tall stature, long arms, aortic root dilation
options.explanation: These are features of Marfan syndrome.
These are features of fragile X or other syndromes.

explanation.overview: Trisomy 18 features: intrauterine growth retardation, micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and overlapping fingers.
explanation.highYield: Edwards syndrome = rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists, low-set ears.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Most infants die within the first year.

questions.question: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is characterized by:

options.explanation: Patau syndrome includes midline defects: cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, and polydactyly.
These are features of Edwards syndrome.
These are features of Down syndrome.
These are features of Turner syndrome.
These are not classic for Patau.

explanation.overview: Patau syndrome includes midline defects: cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, and polydactyly.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Severe malformations, usually lethal in infancy.

questions.question: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with which cardiac abnormality?

options.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve are common in Turner syndrome.
TOF is seen in DiGeorge syndrome.
Pulmonary stenosis is seen in Noonan syndrome.

explanation.overview: Coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve are common in Turner syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac evaluation is crucial in Turner patients.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is characterized by:

options.explanation: Klinefelter males are tall, with small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility due to seminiferous tubule hyalinization.
These are features of Turner syndrome.
These are seen in fragile X or other syndromes.
These are features of Prader-Willi syndrome.

options.text: Long limbs, aortic dilation, lens dislocation
options.explanation: These are features of Marfan syndrome.

explanation.overview: Klinefelter males are tall, with small testes, gynecomastia, and infertility due to seminiferous tubule hyalinization.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Testosterone replacement may help with virilization.

questions.question: The image shows a patient with tall stature, long limbs, and arachnodactyly. This is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Marfan syndrome features tall stature, long extremities, arachnodactyly, and lens dislocation.
Homocystinuria can also cause marfanoid habitus but with intellectual disability and thromboembolism.
Klinefelter causes tall stature but not arachnodactyly or lens dislocation.
Sotos causes overgrowth and macrocephaly, not arachnodactyly.
EDS causes hypermobility and skin laxity, not typically tall stature.

explanation.overview: Marfan syndrome features tall stature, long extremities, arachnodactyly, and lens dislocation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac monitoring for aortic root dilation is essential.

questions.question: The most common cause of short stature in children is:

options.explanation: GHD is a less common cause.
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is a normal variant and the most common cause.
Turner is a genetic cause, less common.
Hypothyroidism is treatable but less common.

explanation.overview: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is a normal variant and the most common cause.
explanation.highYield: Most common short stature = constitutional delay.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Reassurance and observation are appropriate; growth eventually catches up.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of uniparental disomy?

options.explanation: Prader-Willi can result from maternal UPD15, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Angelman can result from paternal UPD15, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Beckwith-Wiedemann can involve paternal UPD11p15, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Prader-Willi is paternal deletion/maternal UPD; Angelman is maternal deletion/paternal UPD; Beckwith-Wiedemann can involve paternal UPD.
These are all imprinting disorders with UPD mechanisms.

explanation.overview: Prader-Willi is paternal deletion/maternal UPD; Angelman is maternal deletion/paternal UPD; Beckwith-Wiedemann can involve paternal UPD.
explanation.highYield: UPD examples: Prader-Willi (maternal UPD15), Angelman (paternal UPD15), Beckwith-Wiedemann (paternal UPD11p15).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Imprinting disorders require understanding of parental origin of genes.

questions.question: Prader-Willi syndrome is most commonly caused by:

options.explanation: This is the most common cause (~70%), but the answer includes both A and C.
This causes Prader-Willi (~25%), but the answer includes both A and C.
Prader-Willi results from loss of paternal genes on 15q11-q13 (deletion or maternal UPD).

explanation.overview: Prader-Willi results from loss of paternal genes on 15q11-q13 (deletion or maternal UPD).
explanation.highYield: Prader-Willi = paternal deletion (70%) or maternal UPD (25%).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Features include hypotonia, obesity, hyperphagia, and intellectual disability.

questions.question: Angelman syndrome is characterized by:

options.text: Happy demeanor, ataxia, severe intellectual disability, seizures
options.explanation: Angelman syndrome (maternal gene loss) causes happy disposition, ataxia, seizures, and severe ID.
These are features of Prader-Willi syndrome.
These are features of fragile X syndrome.

options.text: Short stature, webbed neck, gonadal dysgenesis
options.explanation: These are features of Turner syndrome.
These are features of Huntington disease.

explanation.overview: Angelman syndrome (maternal gene loss) causes happy disposition, ataxia, seizures, and severe ID.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Most cases are due to maternal deletion of 15q11-q13.

questions.question: The gene responsible for Angelman syndrome is:

options.explanation: UBE3A (ubiquitin-protein ligase) is the imprinted gene involved in Angelman syndrome.
SNRPN is imprinted in Prader-Willi syndrome.
FMR1 is involved in fragile X.
DMPK is involved in myotonic dystrophy.

explanation.overview: UBE3A (ubiquitin-protein ligase) is the imprinted gene involved in Angelman syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Maternal copy of UBE3A is active in brain; paternal copy is silenced.

questions.question: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is associated with:

options.text: Overgrowth, macroglossia, omphalocele, predisposition to Wilms tumor
options.explanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann (11p15 imprinting) features neonatal hypoglycemia, macrosomia, abdominal wall defects, and tumor risk.
These are features of many other syndromes.

options.text: Short stature, broad chest, short fingers
Tall stature, long limbs, aortic dilation

explanation.overview: Beckwith-Wiedemann (11p15 imprinting) features neonatal hypoglycemia, macrosomia, abdominal wall defects, and tumor risk.
explanation.highYield: Beckwith-Wiedemann = overgrowth, macroglossia, omphalocele, Wilms tumor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Children need surveillance for embryonal tumors.

questions.question: The most common cause of inherited intellectual disability in males is:

options.explanation: Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability (males more severely affected).
Down is chromosomal, not inherited in the usual sense.

explanation.overview: Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability (males more severely affected).
explanation.highYield: Most common inherited ID in males = fragile X.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing for CGG repeats is diagnostic.

questions.question: Rett syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder affecting:

options.explanation: Rett syndrome (MECP2 mutations) occurs almost exclusively in females, as it is lethal in hemizygous males.
While almost exclusively females, it's not 'only' as rare males with Klinefelter can be affected.

explanation.overview: Rett syndrome (MECP2 mutations) occurs almost exclusively in females, as it is lethal in hemizygous males.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Characterized by loss of milestones, hand-wringing, and microcephaly.

questions.question: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion of chromosome:

options.explanation: Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion) involves 7q11.23, causing supravalvular aortic stenosis, elfin facies, and friendly personality.

explanation.overview: Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion) involves 7q11.23, causing supravalvular aortic stenosis, elfin facies, and friendly personality.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cardiac evaluation and hypercalcemia monitoring are important.

questions.question: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) is characterized by:

options.text: Thymic hypoplasia, parathyroid hypoplasia, cardiac defects
options.explanation: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) includes thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency), hypoparathyroidism, and conotruncal heart defects.

options.text: Tall stature, long limbs, aortic dilation

explanation.overview: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) includes thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency), hypoparathyroidism, and conotruncal heart defects.
explanation.highYield: DiGeorge = 22q11.2 deletion, thymic aplasia, hypoparathyroidism, cardiac defects.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Check calcium and T-cell function; cardiac surgery may be needed.

questions.question: The image shows a conotruncal cardiac defect. Which genetic syndrome is commonly associated?

options.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome frequently causes tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, or interrupted aortic arch.
Down causes AVSD, not typically conotruncal.

explanation.overview: DiGeorge syndrome frequently causes tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, or interrupted aortic arch.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: FISH for 22q11.2 deletion is diagnostic.

questions.question: Noonan syndrome is a disorder that phenotypically resembles:

options.explanation: Noonan syndrome (autosomal dominant) features short stature, webbed neck, pulmonic stenosis, and resembles Turner but with normal karyotype.
Noonan is short stature; Marfan is tall.

explanation.overview: Noonan syndrome (autosomal dominant) features short stature, webbed neck, pulmonic stenosis, and resembles Turner but with normal karyotype.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Caused by mutations in PTPN11 (50%).

questions.question: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by mutation in:

options.explanation: NF1 (17q11.2) encodes neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor.

explanation.overview: NF1 (17q11.2) encodes neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diagnostic criteria include café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules.

questions.question: Diagnostic criteria for NF1 include:

options.text: ≥6 café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas
options.explanation: NF1 criteria include café-au-lait spots, freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic glioma, and bony lesions.

explanation.overview: NF1 criteria include café-au-lait spots, freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic glioma, and bony lesions.
explanation.highYield: NF1 criteria: ≥6 CAL spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Two or more criteria are needed for diagnosis.

questions.question: Neurofibromatosis type 2 is characterized by:

options.explanation: NF2 (22q12) causes bilateral acoustic neuromas (schwannomas), meningiomas, and juvenile cataracts.

explanation.overview: NF2 (22q12) causes bilateral acoustic neuromas (schwannomas), meningiomas, and juvenile cataracts.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MRI is used for surveillance.

questions.question: Tuberous sclerosis is caused by mutations in:

options.explanation: TSC involves hamartin (9q34) or tuberin (16p13) genes, leading to hamartomas in multiple organs.

explanation.overview: TSC involves hamartin (9q34) or tuberin (16p13) genes, leading to hamartomas in multiple organs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Classic triad: seizures, intellectual disability, and facial angiofibromas.

questions.question: Clinical features of tuberous sclerosis include:

options.text: Facial angiofibromas, renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, cortical tubers
options.explanation: TSC causes seizures, intellectual disability, and benign tumors in skin, kidney, heart, and brain.

explanation.overview: TSC causes seizures, intellectual disability, and benign tumors in skin, kidney, heart, and brain.
explanation.highYield: TSC = angiofibromas, angiomyolipomas, rhabdomyomas, cortical tubers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing and imaging are used for diagnosis.

questions.question: The image shows facial angiofibromas in a butterfly distribution. This is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) are seen in tuberous sclerosis.

explanation.overview: Angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) are seen in tuberous sclerosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Often misdiagnosed as acne.

questions.question: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is associated with:

options.text: Hemangioblastomas of CNS and retina, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma
options.explanation: VHL (3p25) is a tumor suppressor gene; loss leads to highly vascular tumors.

explanation.overview: VHL (3p25) is a tumor suppressor gene; loss leads to highly vascular tumors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surveillance for renal and CNS tumors is crucial.

questions.question: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is associated with germline mutations in:

options.explanation: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation) causes predisposition to multiple cancers: sarcomas, breast, brain, leukemia.

explanation.overview: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation) causes predisposition to multiple cancers: sarcomas, breast, brain, leukemia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Intensive cancer surveillance is recommended.

questions.question: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is caused by mutation in:

options.explanation: APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene mutation causes hundreds of colorectal polyps and high cancer risk.

explanation.overview: APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene mutation causes hundreds of colorectal polyps and high cancer risk.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prophylactic colectomy is recommended.

questions.question: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) involves mutations in:

options.text: DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2)
options.explanation: Lynch syndrome results from defective mismatch repair, causing microsatellite instability.

explanation.overview: Lynch syndrome results from defective mismatch repair, causing microsatellite instability.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Screening includes colonoscopy and endometrial surveillance.

questions.question: Retinoblastoma can be hereditary (germline RB1 mutation) or sporadic. Hereditary retinoblastoma is often:

options.explanation: Hereditary retinoblastoma is bilateral/multifocal due to germline mutation and early onset.

explanation.overview: Hereditary retinoblastoma is bilateral/multifocal due to germline mutation and early onset.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients with hereditary Rb are at risk for other cancers (osteosarcoma).

questions.question: The two-hit hypothesis of tumor suppressor genes was first described in:

options.explanation: Knudson's two-hit model explains hereditary vs sporadic retinoblastoma.
Li-Fraumeni also follows two-hit but was not the first.
FAP also follows two-hit but later.
NF also follows two-hit but not first.

explanation.overview: Knudson's two-hit model explains hereditary vs sporadic retinoblastoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In hereditary cases, first hit is germline; second is somatic.

questions.question: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations increase risk for which cancers?

options.explanation: BRCA mutations predispose to breast, ovarian, and other cancers (pancreatic, prostate).

explanation.overview: BRCA mutations predispose to breast, ovarian, and other cancers (pancreatic, prostate).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Risk-reducing surgeries and surveillance are recommended.

questions.question: Cowden syndrome is caused by PTEN mutations and is associated with:

options.explanation: Cowden syndrome features multiple hamartomas and increased risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer.

explanation.overview: Cowden syndrome features multiple hamartomas and increased risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cancer surveillance is essential.

questions.question: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is characterized by:

options.explanation: Peutz-Jeghers (STK11 mutation) causes perioral pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps with increased cancer risk.

options.text: Multiple osteomas, sebaceous cysts, colorectal polyps

explanation.overview: Peutz-Jeghers (STK11 mutation) causes perioral pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps with increased cancer risk.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Increased risk of GI and extra-GI cancers.

questions.question: Gardner syndrome (a variant of FAP) includes:

options.text: Colorectal polyps, osteomas, soft tissue tumors
options.explanation: Gardner syndrome (APC mutation) includes polyposis, osteomas, and soft tissue tumors (desmoids).

explanation.overview: Gardner syndrome (APC mutation) includes polyposis, osteomas, and soft tissue tumors (desmoids).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Desmoids can cause morbidity; prophylactic colectomy is indicated.

questions.question: The image shows a mandibular osteoma. This lesion is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Osteomas are a feature of Gardner syndrome.
McCune-Albright has fibrous dysplasia, not osteomas.
MEN2B has mucosal neuromas, not osteomas.

explanation.overview: Osteomas are a feature of Gardner syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gardner is a variant of FAP with extracolonic manifestations.

questions.question: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) involves mutations in:

options.explanation: MEN1 (11q13) causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors.

explanation.overview: MEN1 (11q13) causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Classic 3 P's: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreatic.

questions.question: MEN2A and MEN2B are caused by mutations in:

options.explanation: RET (rearranged during transfection) is a proto-oncogene mutated in MEN2.

explanation.overview: RET (rearranged during transfection) is a proto-oncogene mutated in MEN2.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prophylactic thyroidectomy may be considered in carriers.

questions.question: MEN2A is characterized by:

options.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia
options.explanation: MEN2A includes MTC, pheo, and hyperparathyroidism. MEN2B has neuromas and marfanoid habitus without parathyroid disease.

options.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus

explanation.overview: MEN2A includes MTC, pheo, and hyperparathyroidism. MEN2B has neuromas and marfanoid habitus without parathyroid disease.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: RET mutation testing guides management.

questions.question: The image shows mucosal neuromas on the tongue. This finding is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Mucosal neuromas are a feature of MEN2B.
MEN2A does not have mucosal neuromas.
NF has neurofibromas, not mucosal neuromas.
Cowden has hamartomas, not mucosal neuromas.

explanation.overview: Mucosal neuromas are a feature of MEN2B.
explanation.highYield: MEN2B = mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, MTC, pheochromocytoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MEN2B is more aggressive; prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended.

questions.question: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by:

options.text: Postzygotic activating mutation in GNAS1 gene
options.explanation: McCune-Albright (fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, precocious puberty) results from somatic activating GNAS mutation.

explanation.overview: McCune-Albright (fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, precocious puberty) results from somatic activating GNAS mutation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment is symptomatic; endocrine manifestations require management.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a disorder caused by genomic imprinting?

options.explanation: Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
Yes, but the answer is 'All of the above'.
All three are imprinting disorders involving chromosome 15q11-q13 or 11p15.

explanation.overview: All three are imprinting disorders involving chromosome 15q11-q13 or 11p15.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Understanding parental origin is key for diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a mitochondrial inheritance disorder?

options.explanation: LHON is caused by mitochondrial DNA mutations, showing maternal inheritance.

explanation.overview: LHON is caused by mitochondrial DNA mutations, showing maternal inheritance.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Maternal inheritance; affected males cannot transmit to offspring.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of MELAS syndrome?

options.text: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes
options.explanation: MELAS is a mitochondrial disorder with these features.

explanation.overview: MELAS is a mitochondrial disorder with these features.
explanation.highYield: MELAS = mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diagnosis via muscle biopsy and genetic testing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a microdeletion syndrome?

options.explanation: Cri-du-chat is a microdeletion of chromosome 5p, causing cat-like cry and intellectual disability.

explanation.overview: Cri-du-chat is a microdeletion of chromosome 5p, causing cat-like cry and intellectual disability.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Characteristic high-pitched cry.

questions.question: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome is caused by deletion of:

options.explanation: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome results from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4.

explanation.overview: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome results from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Features: intellectual disability, microcephaly, cleft lip/palate.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a disorder with variable expressivity?

options.explanation: NF1 exhibits marked variable expressivity; affected individuals can have mild to severe manifestations.
Tay-Sachs is generally consistent in severity.
CF has some variability, but NF1 is a classic example.
Duchenne has a relatively predictable course.

explanation.overview: NF1 exhibits marked variable expressivity; affected individuals can have mild to severe manifestations.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Family members may have different features despite same mutation.

questions.question: Penetrance refers to:

options.text: The proportion of individuals with a mutation who show any signs of the disease
options.explanation: Penetrance is the likelihood that a gene mutation will cause any phenotype.
Age of onset is not penetrance.

options.text: The number of affected family members

options.explanation: Penetrance is not about mutation type.

explanation.overview: Penetrance is the likelihood that a gene mutation will cause any phenotype.
explanation.highYield: Penetrance = proportion with mutation who express phenotype.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Reduced penetrance is seen in BRCA and other cancer syndromes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a disorder with reduced penetrance?

options.explanation: BRCA mutations have reduced penetrance; not all carriers develop cancer.
Huntington has complete penetrance if repeat is expanded.

explanation.overview: BRCA mutations have reduced penetrance; not all carriers develop cancer.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Risk assessment and surveillance are tailored to penetrance.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer is found to have a BRCA1 mutation. This is an example of:

options.explanation: BRCA mutations cause hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.
This is a germline mutation, not somatic.
It is inherited from a parent.

explanation.overview: BRCA mutations cause hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing, counseling, and risk-reducing surgeries are options.

questions.question: The pharmacogenetics of TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) is important for which drug?

options.explanation: TPMT metabolizes thiopurines; deficiency leads to myelotoxicity.
Warfarin is metabolized by CYP2C9 and VKORC1.

explanation.overview: TPMT metabolizes thiopurines; deficiency leads to myelotoxicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: TPMT testing before starting thiopurines can prevent severe toxicity.

questions.question: CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect the metabolism of which drug?

options.explanation: CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine and activates tamoxifen.

explanation.overview: CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine and activates tamoxifen.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Poor metabolizers may not get pain relief or benefit from tamoxifen.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome?

options.explanation: Prader-Willi features: neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and mild ID.

explanation.overview: Prader-Willi features: neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and mild ID.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Growth hormone therapy and dietary management are important.

questions.question: Which of the following is a trinucleotide repeat disorder that affects the cerebellum?

options.explanation: Many SCAs are caused by CAG repeat expansions.
Fragile X affects brain development, not primarily cerebellum.
Myotonic dystrophy affects muscle, not cerebellum.
Huntington affects basal ganglia, not cerebellum.
Friedreich affects spinal cord and cerebellum but is GAA repeat, not CAG.

explanation.overview: Many SCAs are caused by CAG repeat expansions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing for specific SCA subtypes is available.

questions.question: Hereditary spastic paraplegia is often inherited in which pattern?

options.text: Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked
options.explanation: HSP is genetically heterogeneous with all three inheritance patterns.

explanation.overview: HSP is genetically heterogeneous with all three inheritance patterns.
explanation.highYield: HSP can be AD, AR, or X-linked.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing panels are available.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a contiguous gene syndrome?

options.explanation: DiGeorge is a contiguous gene deletion affecting multiple genes.
Huntington is a single gene disorder.

explanation.overview: DiGeorge is a contiguous gene deletion affecting multiple genes.
explanation.highYield: Contiguous gene syndromes: DiGeorge, Williams, Prader-Willi/Angelman.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Microarray analysis can detect these deletions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Noonan syndrome?

options.text: Short stature, webbed neck, pulmonic stenosis, cryptorchidism
options.explanation: Noonan syndrome includes these features and a normal karyotype.

options.text: Tall stature, aortic root dilation, lens subluxation

explanation.overview: Noonan syndrome includes these features and a normal karyotype.
explanation.highYield: Noonan = short, webbed neck, pulmonic stenosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in PTPN11 and other genes cause Noonan.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disorder of imprinting involving chromosome 15?

options.explanation: Both are due to abnormalities of 15q11-q13.

explanation.overview: Both are due to abnormalities of 15q11-q13.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Parental origin of deletion determines which syndrome.

questions.question: A patient with a family history of early-onset colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, and ovarian cancer is most likely to have which syndrome?

options.explanation: Lynch syndrome (MMR mutations) predisposes to colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, and other cancers.
FAP causes many polyps but not endometrial/ovarian.
BRCA predisposes to breast and ovarian, not colorectal.

explanation.overview: Lynch syndrome (MMR mutations) predisposes to colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, and other cancers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tumor testing for MSI and IHC for MMR proteins is recommended.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC)?

options.text: CDH1 mutations, diffuse (signet ring) gastric cancer, lobular breast cancer
options.explanation: HDGC is caused by CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutations.

explanation.overview: HDGC is caused by CDH1 (E-cadherin) mutations.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prophylactic gastrectomy is offered to carriers.

questions.question: Which of the following is a genetic disorder of connective tissue that can cause aortic dissection?

options.text: Marfan syndrome and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

options.explanation: OI causes brittle bones, not aortic dissection.
Classic EDS does not typically cause aortic dissection.
Homocystinuria can cause thrombosis, not typically aortic dissection.

explanation.overview: Both predispose to aortic dissection.
explanation.highYield: Aortic dissection risk: Marfan, vascular EDS.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Blood pressure control and surgical repair are key.

questions.question: Which of the following is a hallmark of Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome?

options.text: Broad thumbs and toes, intellectual disability, characteristic facies
options.explanation: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome is caused by mutations in CREBBP or EP300.

explanation.overview: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome is caused by mutations in CREBBP or EP300.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Genetic testing can confirm.

questions.question: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is associated with mutations in:

options.explanation: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is due to mutations in cohesin complex genes.

explanation.overview: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is due to mutations in cohesin complex genes.
explanation.highYield: Cornelia de Lange = NIPBL, SMC1A, SMC3.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Features: intellectual disability, limb anomalies, characteristic facies.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of CHARGE syndrome?

options.text: Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth, Genital anomalies, Ear abnormalities
options.explanation: CHARGE is caused by CHD7 mutations.

explanation.overview: CHARGE is caused by CHD7 mutations.
explanation.highYield: CHARGE = Coloboma, Heart, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth, Genital, Ear.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Multidisciplinary care is needed.

questions.question: A patient with hearing loss, renal failure, and ocular abnormalities likely has:

options.explanation: Alport syndrome (COL4A5) affects kidney, ear, and eye.
Marfan affects eye and heart, not kidney.
TSC affects brain, skin, kidney, but not hearing.

explanation.overview: Alport syndrome (COL4A5) affects kidney, ear, and eye.
explanation.highYield: Alport = nephritis + hearing loss + ocular abnormalities.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Renal biopsy shows basement membrane splitting.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of Fabry disease?

options.text: α-galactosidase A deficiency, angiokeratomas, renal failure, neuropathy
options.explanation: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder.

explanation.overview: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Enzyme replacement therapy is available.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Gaucher disease?

options.text: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency, Gaucher cells in bone marrow, hepatosplenomegaly
options.explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.

explanation.overview: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Enzyme replacement therapy is effective.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Niemann-Pick disease types A and B?

options.text: Sphingomyelinase deficiency, foam cells, hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration (type A)
options.explanation: Niemann-Pick is due to acid sphingomyelinase deficiency.

explanation.overview: Niemann-Pick is due to acid sphingomyelinase deficiency.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Type A is severe neurodegenerative; type B is milder with visceral involvement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disorder of mucopolysaccharide metabolism?

options.explanation: Hurler is due to α-L-iduronidase deficiency.
PKU is an amino acid disorder.

explanation.overview: Hurler is due to α-L-iduronidase deficiency.
explanation.highYield: MPS disorders: Hurler (MPS I), Hunter (MPS II), Sanfilippo (MPS III).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant may be used.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Hunter syndrome (MPS II)?

options.text: X-linked inheritance, iduronate sulfatase deficiency, coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly

explanation.overview: Hunter syndrome is X-linked MPS.
explanation.highYield: Hunter = MPS II, X-linked, iduronate sulfatase.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Enzyme replacement and stem cell transplant are options.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS III)?

options.text: Heparan sulfate accumulation, severe intellectual disability, mild somatic features
options.explanation: Sanfilippo is due to deficiency of enzymes involved in heparan sulfate degradation.
This is more typical of Hurler/Hunter.

explanation.overview: Sanfilippo is due to deficiency of enzymes involved in heparan sulfate degradation.
explanation.highYield: Sanfilippo = MPS III, heparan sulfate, severe ID.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mainly neurologic involvement; no effective treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Morquio syndrome (MPS IV)?

options.text: Keratan sulfate accumulation, skeletal dysplasia, odontoid hypoplasia, corneal clouding
options.explanation: Morquio syndrome affects skeletal system and cornea.

explanation.overview: Morquio syndrome affects skeletal system and cornea.
explanation.highYield: Morquio = MPS IV, keratan sulfate, odontoid hypoplasia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cervical spine instability requires careful management.
